locations.note: Chariot on the desert road where the eunuch reads Isaiah and is baptized (Acts 8:28-38).

locations.name: Water beside the road
locations.note: Place on the desert road where the eunuch is baptized (Acts 8:36-38).

locations.name: The riverside outside Philippi
aliases: the place of prayer by the river
locations.note: Riverbank outside the gate where Paul speaks to women and Lydia is baptized (Acts 16:13).

locations.name: Philippi
locations.note: Roman colony where Lydia, the slave girl, Paul and Silas, and the jailer appear (Acts 16:12-40).

locations.name: The prison at Philippi
locations.note: Inner prison where Paul and Silas are held in stocks and freed by earthquake (Acts 16:23-34).

locations.name: The marketplace of Philippi
locations.note: Public square where Paul and Silas are dragged before the magistrates (Acts 16:19).

locations.name: Thessalonica
locations.note: City with a Jewish synagogue where Paul preaches three Sabbaths and Jason's house is attacked (Acts 17:1-9).

locations.name: Jason's house in Thessalonica
locations.note: House attacked by the mob (Acts 17:5).

locations.name: Beroea
locations.note: City where Jews examine the Scriptures daily and believe (Acts 17:10-14).

locations.name: Athens
locations.note: City full of idols where Paul debates in the synagogue and marketplace (Acts 17:16-34).

locations.name: The Areopagus
locations.note: Hill and council place in Athens where Paul speaks about the unknown god (Acts 17:19-34).

locations.name: Corinth
locations.note: City where Paul lives eighteen months with Aquila and Priscilla and faces the case before Gallio (Acts 18:1-17).

locations.name: House of Justus next to the synagogue in Corinth
locations.note: House beside the synagogue where Paul teaches (Acts 18:7).

locations.name: The judgment seat at Corinth
locations.note: Court where Gallio dismisses the charges against Paul (Acts 18:12-17).

locations.name: Cenchreae
locations.note: Port near Corinth where Paul shaves his head for a vow (Acts 18:18).

locations.name: Ephesus
locations.note: City where Paul spends two years, the sons of Sceva are beaten, and the silversmith riot occurs (Acts 18:19-19:41).

locations.name: School of Tyrannus
locations.note: Lecture hall in Ephesus where Paul reasons daily (Acts 19:9).

locations.name: The theater at Ephesus
locations.note: Theater where the silversmiths' mob gathers and cries for Artemis (Acts 19:29-41).

locations.name: Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
aliases: the temple of the great goddess Artemis
locations.note: Great temple whose shrines and worship are threatened (Acts 19:27).

locations.name: Macedonia
locations.note: Region visited by Paul on his journeys, including Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea (Acts 16:9-17:14, 19:21-20:3).

locations.name: Troas
locations.note: Port where Paul receives the Macedonian vision and where Eutychus falls from the window (Acts 16:8, 20:5-12).

locations.name: Upper room at Troas
aliases: the upper room where we were gathered
locations.note: Room with many lamps where Paul speaks late and Eutychus falls (Acts 20:7-9).

locations.name: Miletus
locations.note: Port where Paul meets the Ephesian elders for farewell (Acts 20:15-38).

locations.name: Tyre
locations.note: Port where Paul's company stays seven days and the believers pray on the beach (Acts 21:3-6).

locations.name: The beach at Tyre
locations.note: Shore where Paul kneels with the disciples and they pray (Acts 21:5).

locations.name: Ptolemais
locations.note: Port where the company greets the brothers for one day (Acts 21:7).

locations.name: Court of the temple
locations.note: Place where Paul is seized by the Asian Jews and nearly killed (Acts 21:27-36).

locations.name: The Roman barracks
locations.note: Roman fortress where Paul is taken under guard (Acts 21:34-37, 22:24, 23:10, 16).

locations.name: Stairs of the fortress
locations.note: Steps from which Paul addresses the crowd in Hebrew (Acts 21:40-22:21).

locations.name: Antipatris
locations.note: Stop on the night road from Jerusalem to Caesarea (Acts 23:31).

locations.name: Fair Havens near Lasea, Crete
locations.note: Harbor on Crete where the ship stays and Paul gives advice (Acts 27:8-12).

locations.name: The ship bound for Italy
locations.note: Ship carrying Paul and the prisoners to Italy, wrecked near Malta (Acts 27:1-44).

locations.name: Malta
locations.note: Island where the ship is wrecked and Paul heals the father of Publius (Acts 28:1-10).

locations.name: Syracuse, Rhegium, Puteoli
locations.note: Ports on the Italian voyage (Acts 28:12-14).

locations.name: Rome
locations.note: Paul's final destination where he is held under guard in his rented house and preaches freely (Acts 28:14-31).

locations.name: The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns
locations.note: Roadside stops where Roman brothers meet Paul (Acts 28:15).

locations.name: Paul's rented house in Rome
locations.note: House where Paul receives visitors for two years (Acts 28:30).

locations.name: Tarsus
locations.note: Paul's birthplace, to which he is sent away from Jerusalem by the brothers (Acts 9:11, 30; 11:25; 21:39; 22:3).

locations.name: Gaza
locations.note: City at the end of the desert road from Jerusalem (Acts 8:26).

locations.name: Cyprus
locations.note: Island visited by Barnabas and Paul; home of Barnabas and Mnason (Acts 4:36, 11:20, 13:4-12, 15:39, 21:16).

locations.name: Salamis and Paphos
locations.note: Cypriot cities visited by Barnabas, Paul and John Mark, where Elymas is blinded (Acts 13:5-12).

locations.name: Perga in Pamphylia
locations.note: Cities where John Mark leaves the missionaries and where they preach (Acts 13:13, 14:25).

locations.name: Antioch of Pisidia
locations.note: Synagogue city where Paul preaches a long sermon on the Sabbath (Acts 13:14-52).

locations.name: Iconium
locations.note: City of Lycaonia where Paul and Barnabas preach, are opposed and flee (Acts 13:51-14:6).

locations.name: Lystra
locations.note: City of Lycaonia where Paul heals the lame man and is stoned (Acts 14:6-20; 16:1-2).

locations.name: Derbe
locations.note: City of Lycaonia where Paul and Barnabas make many disciples (Acts 14:6, 20; 16:1; 20:4).

locations.name: Lycaonia
locations.note: Region including Lystra, Derbe and Iconium where Paul is taken for Hermes (Acts 14:6-11).

locations.name: Phrygia and Galatia
aliases: the region of Galatia and Phrygia
locations.note: Regions traversed by Paul on the journeys (Acts 16:6, 18:23).

locations.name: Mysia and Bithynia
locations.note: Regions Paul is forbidden to enter (Acts 16:7-8).

locations.name: Asia
locations.note: Roman province where Paul is forbidden to speak and later ministers in Ephesus (Acts 16:6, 19:10, 20:18).

locations.name: The burning bush
locations.note: Place of the angel's appearance to Moses (Acts 7:30-33).

locations.name: Roman provinces of Achaia and Macedonia
locations.note: Provinces through which Paul travels to Corinth and Achaia (Acts 18:12, 19:21, 20:2-3).

locations.name: Italy
locations.note: Region toward which Paul is sent, and from which Aquila and Priscilla came (Acts 18:2, 27:1).

locations.name: The sea
aliases: the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia
locations.note: Several seas referred to in the narrative, including the sea of the shipwreck (Acts 27:27) and the Red Sea (Acts 7:36).

locations.name: Outside the city wall of Jerusalem
locations.note: Place where Stephen is stoned after being cast out (Acts 7:58).

locations.name: The wall of Damascus
locations.note: Wall through which Saul is lowered in a basket (Acts 9:25).

locations.name: Gate of Damascus
locations.note: Gate watched by the Jews who plot to kill Saul (Acts 9:24).

locations.name: Shipwreck site near the island
locations.note: Coast where the ship runs aground and the passengers reach land (Acts 27:39-44).

locations.name: Hall of hearing in Caesarea
locations.note: Official hall where Festus brings Paul before Agrippa and Bernice (Acts 25:23).

locations.name: The judgment seat in Caesarea
locations.note: Tribunal where Festus sits and Paul is brought (Acts 25:6, 17).

locations.name: Gate of the temple
locations.note: Temple gate where Peter and John meet the lame man (Acts 3:2; cf. Beautiful Gate); included for the setting of Acts 3.

locations.name: The house of Philip the evangelist
locations.note: Caesarean house where Paul stays with Philip and his four prophesying daughters (Acts 21:8-10).

locations.name: House where the apostles met
aliases: the apostles and elders' meeting place
locations.note: Place in Jerusalem where the council of Acts 15 is held; not separately named in the text.

locations.name: House of Judas in Damascus
locations.note: House on Straight Street where Saul is kept three days blind (Acts 9:11).

GEN.tone: Ancient, solemn and intimate: a primordial beginning followed by family dramas of blessing, betrayal, reconciliation and promise.
depiction_rules: God is not given a human face or body; show him by light, voice, a cloud or a hand where tradition permits, and angels as luminous messengers.
Show the tree of life and knowledge and the serpent with restraint; the serpent may be drawn as a plain animal.
Do not depict the nakedness of Noah, Ham, Lot or Lot's daughters explicitly; cover or turn figures away.
Lot's wife may be shown as a pillar of salt without gore.
Depict the flood, Sodom and the binding of Isaac with weight and dignity, without gratuitous violence.

era.name: The ancient Near East, from the primeval world through the patriarchal age to Egypt in the Middle or Late Bronze Age
era.people: Semitic herders, farmers and city dwellers of Mesopotamia, Canaan, and Egypt; Egyptians, Philistines, Hittites and Canaanites appear in the narrative. People have dark hair and beards for men and wear simple, earth-toned clothing.
era.dress: Simple linen or wool tunics and robes, cloaks and head coverings, sandals; Egyptian officials in fine linen with gold chains; women veiled in the presence of men.
era.buildings_and_objects: Mud-brick and stone cities such as Ur, tents of goat hair for nomads, altars of stone, wells, vineyards, flocks, camels and donkeys, chariots in Egypt.
era.technology: Bronze and early iron tools, pottery, weaving and the potter's wheel; no writing of the text itself at the time described, no firearms, no metal coins (silver is weighed by the shekel).

EXO.tone: Awe and sacred dread in the plague and mountain scenes, grief and tension in the flight, and warm, devotional calm in the craft and law passages.
depiction_rules: Yahweh is never given a human face or full body; show him as a voice, a burning bush, a pillar of cloud or fire, or the glory filling the tabernacle.
Moses' face shines after Sinai; render as a radiance or veil rather than a literal glow.
The plagues are shown as they occur in the text, with the river blood, swarms, hail, locusts, and darkness, without gratuitous gore beyond the death of the firstborn.
The golden calf is an idol to be shown as a molten calf, not as a god.
The Passover blood on doorposts is shown on lintel and posts only.
Laws and ritual instructions can be shown as objects and settings, not as literal legal scenes.

era.name: Late Bronze Age Egypt, Sinai, and the Sinai wilderness
era.people: Egyptians with shaven heads, linen kilts and wigs, and Hebrew clans in simple desert clothing, dark-haired and bearded; Midianite shepherds.
era.dress: Linen kilts and tunics for Egyptians; plain woven wool and linen for Israelites; priestly garments of blue, purple, scarlet and gold-threaded linen with an ephod, breastplate and bells.
era.buildings_and_objects: Brick storage cities such as Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh; tents and a portable tabernacle with acacia boards, gold-overlaid ark, lampstand, altars and bronze court; papyrus baskets, clay kneading troughs, rods and staves.
era.technology: Brickmaking with straw and mortar, chariots and horses in the Egyptian army, bronze and gold metalwork, weaving and embroidery, fire and oil lamps; no iron tools, writing on stone tablets, and no coinage (weights are used).

1SA.tone: Austere, tense and intimate: a book of prophecy, kingship and fraught loyalty, with grief and dread in quiet interiors and bursts of violence on open fields.
depiction_rules: Yahweh is never shown in human or animal form; depict only effects (a voice, light, thunder, the ark) rather than a visible deity.
The ark of the covenant may be depicted as a gold-covered chest with cherubim, not as a person.
Dagon, the Ashtaroth and the teraphim are idols and may be shown as statues without divine presence.
The Philistine champion Goliath is a fully armed giant; the raw violence of the sling stone and beheading may be shown but without gratuitous gore.
The Woman of Endor's necromancy is shown with Samuel as an old robed figure rising from the ground, not as a dramatic demonic spectacle.
Nudity (Saul prophesying naked, 19:24) may be depicted with restraint.

era.name: Late Bronze to early Iron Age Israel and Philistia, c. 11th century BCE
era.people: Israelite tribes (Ephraimites, Benjamites, Judahites) living as farmers and herders in hill country; Philistines as an organized city-state people with bronze and iron weapons; neighbors include Ammonites, Moabites, Amalekites and Edomites.
era.dress: Linen ephods for priests and boys; robes and mantles for elders and kings; bronze helmets and coats of mail for warriors; shepherds' bags and slings; simple woven tunics for common people.
era.buildings_and_objects: Mud-brick and stone houses with flat roofs; the tabernacle at Shiloh with doorposts and gates; altars of stone; the wooden ark overlaid with gold; threshing floors; watchtowers and strongholds; caves used as refuges.
era.technology: Bronze and emerging iron weapons and tools (iron spearheads, blacksmiths are rare among Israel); chariots and horses used by Philistines; oil lamps and horns for anointing; no writing of a full literary kind beyond scribal notes, but a book of royal law is written.

MAT.tone: Reverent and luminous in the miracles and birth scenes, grave and sorrowful through the passion, with austere moral weight in the teaching discourses.
depiction_rules: Show Jesus as central and always identifiable; avoid depicting God the Father directly, use a voice from the cloud or light.
Angels appear as luminous human-like messengers, not winged cherubs drawn from later tradition unless the scene calls for it.
Depict the Holy Spirit as a dove in the baptism scene only, as the text describes.
The crucifixion may be shown but without gratuitous gore; the veil torn and the darkness are depicted as signs, not spectacle.
Parables are shown as realistic scenes of rural and town life of the period rather than allegorical symbols.
Avoid antisemitic caricature of Pharisees, scribes and crowds; show them as individuals with varied expressions.

era.name: First-century Roman Judea and Galilee
era.people: Jewish villagers, fishermen, shepherds, tax collectors, Roman soldiers and officials, Pharisees and priests in traditional dress; Gentiles from Tyre, Sidon and Syria appear in some scenes.
era.dress: Tunics and cloaks with fringed garments, head coverings, sandals, linen and wool; Roman soldiers in armor and tunics; priests in linen robes; women with veils.
era.buildings_and_objects: Stone and mud-brick houses with flat roofs, village synagogues, the Jerusalem temple with courts and veil, marketplaces, vineyards, threshing floors, fishing boats and nets, oil lamps, clay jars, tombs cut in rock.
era.technology: No gunpowder, printing or clocks; oil lamps, boats with sails and oars, hand mills, ox carts, coins such as denarii and shekels. Writing exists on scrolls and parchment.

LUK.tone: Reverent, quiet and luminous: intimate household scenes beside public crowds, with angelic light and dusk over Jerusalem, and grief giving way to hope.
depiction_rules: Show Jesus as a human figure without a fixed face-type rule beyond the era's appearance; avoid halos unless the scene demands a glory motif.
The divine voice and angels should appear through light, cloud, and posture rather than literal flesh where possible.
Satan and demons may be shown as dark or distorted presences, not as detailed monsters.
Violence (the crucifixion, the beheading referred to by Herod) is restrained and not gratuitous.
Women are present throughout and should be drawn as full participants, including in the nativity, the healing, and the resurrection.
Avoid depicting Jesus' mother with a mother-and-child emphasis that goes beyond the text.

era.name: First-century Roman Judea and Galilee
era.people: Jewish villagers, farmers, fishermen, shepherds, tax collectors, priests, Pharisees and Sadducees, Roman soldiers and officials, Samaritans and Gentiles; people of the Eastern Mediterranean with olive, brown and dark hair and tanned skin.
era.dress: Linen and wool tunics, cloaks and mantles (himation), head coverings and veils for women, phylacteries and tassels for devout men; priests in white linen; Roman soldiers in armor and tunics; tax collectors and wealthy in purple and fine linen.
era.buildings_and_objects: Stone and mud-brick houses with flat roofs and tiled roofs, the Herodian temple in Jerusalem, synagogues, tombs cut into rock with rolling stones, oil lamps, feeding troughs, fishing boats and nets, threshing floors, vineyards, sycamore and fig trees, cups and bread, scrolls.
era.technology: No printing, clocks, or machinery; no firearms; writing on scrolls and wax or wooden tablets; Roman roads and coins (denarii); lamps, plows, looms; no photography or mechanical transport beyond boats and animals.

JHN.tone: Contemplative and luminous, with a sense of divine glory breaking into ordinary life; quiet intimacy in dialogue scenes and tension in conflict scenes.
depiction_rules: Depict Jesus as a Jewish man of the 1st century, not with the halo-and-blue-robe stereotype of later art unless the illustration calls for it.
Show the divine voice from the sky and the angels in white as light rather than as human figures where possible.
Handle the crucifixion with restraint, avoiding gratuitous gore while keeping its weight.
Do not depict God the Father in human form.
Show the Holy Spirit as a dove or as wind/breath only where the text names it.
Avoid caricaturing Jews, Pharisees and Judas; depict the opponents as religious authorities and crowds with individual dignity.

era.name: Roman Judea and Galilee, c. AD 30
era.people: Jewish villagers, fishermen, priests, Pharisees, Samaritans, Roman soldiers and officials; mostly brown-skinned Mediterranean people with dark hair and beards for men.
era.dress: Linen tunics, woolen cloaks and mantles, head coverings, sandals; priests in linen robes; Roman soldiers in armor and tunic; purple garment as mock royalty.
era.buildings_and_objects: Stone houses with flat roofs, village wells, stone water jars, the Jerusalem temple and its courts, synagogues, rock-cut tombs closed by a rolled stone, lamps, nets and boats on the Sea of Galilee, olive groves and vineyards.
era.technology: Oil lamps, torches, handmade boats and nets, hand-milled grain and baked bread, wine and oil; no photography, no printed books, no firearms, no clocks; Roman roads and governor's praetorium exist.

ACT.tone: Hopeful and urgent: a young movement spreading outward from Jerusalem, marked by miracles, fierce opposition, courtroom tension, and quiet communal devotion.
depiction_rules: Depict the risen Jesus only in the Acts 1 ascension and in Saul's vision; do not show a face or body for God the Father, only light, cloud or a hand.
The Holy Spirit appears as wind, tongues of fire or a dove-like presence, not as a human figure.
Angels appear as men in white or bright clothing, as the text describes them.
Show miracles (healing, the earthquake, the viper) as events in the scene, not as spectacle; avoid gore in the stoning and the death of Ananias and Sapphira beyond the implied moment.
Avoid depicting Judas's death in detail; the text describes it only in speech.
Show the crowds at Ephesus and Jerusalem as agitated but not caricatured.

era.name: First-century Roman Empire, c. AD 30-62, from Jerusalem and Judea to Rome
era.people: Jews of Galilee and Judea, Hellenistic Jews of the diaspora, Samaritans, Greeks, Romans, Cypriots, Lycaonians, Ethiopians, and islanders of Malta; Roman officials, soldiers and sailors; many languages in use.
era.dress: Robes and cloaks (himation, tunics), head coverings for men and women, sandals, belts, military Roman tunics and cloaks for soldiers, white garments for angels and priests, sailors in short tunics.
era.buildings_and_objects: Jerusalem temple and its porches and gates, synagogues, upper rooms with lamps, Roman barracks and governors' palaces such as Herod's palace at Caesarea, city gates and walls, Greek theaters and temples (Artemis at Ephesus), ships with sails and anchors, chariots, scrolls and letters.
era.technology: Sailing ships and oared vessels, lamps and oil light, carts and chariots, scrolls and written letters, no printing, no firearms, no mechanical clocks; time reckoned by hours of the day.

clusters.name: God (Yahweh)
clusters.note: The creator God of Genesis and the God of Israel who speaks and acts across the Hebrew Bible and Acts; the same divine presence under each title and every book.

clusters.name: Abram / Abraham the patriarch
clusters.note: Son of Terah, called from Haran and renamed Abraham; the patriarch of Genesis, mentioned as father in the Gospels and Acts.

clusters.name: Simeon son of Jacob
clusters.note: Son of Jacob and Leah, involved in the Shechem massacre and held by Joseph in Egypt.

clusters.name: Simeon the righteous man
clusters.note: Devout man in Jerusalem who blesses the infant Jesus in the temple; distinct from the patriarch Simeon.

clusters.name: Levi son of Jacob
clusters.note: Son of Jacob and Leah, who with Simeon avenges Dinah; a patriarch of Genesis, not a tax collector.

clusters.name: Matthew / Levi the tax collector
clusters.note: Tax collector called to follow Jesus, named Matthew in Matthew and Levi in Luke; also the apostle Matthew in the apostle lists.

clusters.name: Gad son of Jacob
clusters.note: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, a patriarch named in Genesis.

clusters.name: Gad the prophet
clusters.note: Prophet who advises David to leave the stronghold; not a son of Jacob.

clusters.name: Joseph son of Jacob
clusters.note: Son of Jacob and Rachel, sold into Egypt and later vizier to Pharaoh; Genesis figure, also recounted by Stephen.

clusters.name: Joseph husband of Mary
clusters.note: Carpenter of Nazareth, husband of Mary and foster father of Jesus, of David's house.

clusters.name: Joseph of Arimathaea
clusters.note: Council member who asks Pilate for Jesus' body and buries him; distinct from the husband of Mary.

clusters.name: Moses
clusters.note: Hebrew leader who leads Israel out of Egypt and receives the law; appears in the Gospels and Acts as the lawgiver.

clusters.name: Pharaoh of the Exodus
clusters.note: The Egyptian king who enslaves Israel and resists the plagues, also referenced by Stephen.

clusters.name: Miriam
clusters.note: Sister of Moses and Aaron and prophetess who leads the song after the sea crossing; likely the same as the sister who watches the basket.

clusters.name: Amalekites
clusters.note: People who attack Israel at Rephidim and later raid Ziklag; the same nation in both books.

clusters.name: Samuel
clusters.note: Prophet and judge who anoints Saul and David, son of Hannah.

clusters.name: Hophni
clusters.note: Wicked son of Eli, priest at Shiloh, killed at Aphek.

clusters.name: Phinehas son of Eli
clusters.note: Wicked son of Eli, killed with Hophni at Aphek; not the later Phinehas son of Eleazar.

clusters.name: Saul the king
clusters.note: First king of Israel, son of Kish, rejected by Samuel and dying on Gilboa.

clusters.name: Saul of Tarsus / Paul
clusters.note: Pharisee persecutor converted on the road to Damascus, later the apostle Paul; the main figure of Acts from chapter 7 on.

clusters.name: Jonathan son of Saul
clusters.note: Eldest son of Saul and close friend of David, who dies on Gilboa.

clusters.name: Ishvi son of Saul
clusters.note: Son of Saul named in a genealogy, killed on Gilboa with Jonathan.

clusters.name: Malchishua son of Saul
clusters.note: Son of Saul killed on Gilboa with Jonathan.

clusters.name: David king of Israel
clusters.note: Youngest son of Jesse, anointed by Samuel, slayer of Goliath and king of Israel; appears as king in the Gospels and Acts.

clusters.name: Abinadab son of Jesse
clusters.note: Brother of David who passed before Samuel; not the Abinadab who hosted the ark.

clusters.name: Shammah son of Jesse
clusters.note: Brother of David who passed before Samuel and fought with Saul.

clusters.name: Joel son of Samuel
clusters.note: Eldest son of Samuel, a corrupt judge at Beersheba.

clusters.name: Abijah son of Samuel
clusters.note: Second son of Samuel, a corrupt judge at Beersheba.

clusters.name: Israelite army and people
clusters.note: The Israelite army and assembly in 1 Samuel acting collectively.

clusters.name: Jerusalem temple crowd
clusters.note: Jews from Asia and the crowd who seize Paul in the temple in Acts 21.

clusters.name: Jesus of Nazareth
clusters.note: Central figure of the Gospels and Acts, the crucified and risen Christ; the same figure across Matthew, Luke, John and Acts.

clusters.name: Blind man of Jericho
clusters.note: Unnamed blind beggar near Jericho who receives sight in Luke 18; distinct from Bartimaeus.

clusters.name: Mary mother of Jesus
clusters.note: Mother of Jesus, betrothed to Joseph, present at Cana, the cross and the upper room.

clusters.name: Mary Magdalene
clusters.note: Woman healed of seven demons who witnesses the crucifixion and the empty tomb.

clusters.name: Mary of Bethany
clusters.note: Sister of Martha and Lazarus who sits at Jesus' feet and anoints him; not the mother of Jesus.

clusters.name: Mary the mother of James
clusters.note: Woman who goes to the tomb and tells the apostles, distinct from Mary the mother of Jesus in Luke's text.

clusters.name: Mary mother of John Mark
clusters.note: Woman in Jerusalem whose house hosts the praying believers in Acts 12.

clusters.name: Herod the Great
clusters.note: King of Judea who seeks the child Jesus and orders the killing of boys in Bethlehem.

clusters.name: Herod Antipas the tetrarch
clusters.note: Tetrarch of Galilee who executes John the Baptizer and mocks Jesus; son of Herod the Great.

clusters.name: Herod Agrippa I
clusters.note: King who kills James and imprisons Peter in Acts 12, struck dead by an angel; distinct from Herod Antipas.

clusters.name: John the Baptizer
clusters.note: Preacher in the wilderness who baptizes Jesus and is imprisoned and beheaded by Herod Antipas.

clusters.name: John the apostle son of Zebedee
clusters.note: Apostle and brother of James, one of the inner three disciples and companion of Peter in Acts.

clusters.name: Pharisees
clusters.note: Religious leaders who repeatedly oppose or question Jesus across the Gospels.

clusters.name: Sadducees
clusters.note: Religious party who deny the resurrection and question Jesus about it.

clusters.name: Scribes / teachers of the law
clusters.note: Teachers of the law who debate Jesus and join the chief priests against him.

clusters.name: The lawyer who tests Jesus
clusters.note: Single scribe who asks Jesus which commandment is greatest; a member of the scribes.

clusters.name: Satan (the devil)
clusters.note: The adversary who tempts Jesus in the wilderness and is called the prince of demons; the same figure in Matthew and Luke.

clusters.name: Simon Peter
clusters.note: Fisherman from Galilee, first called disciple and apostle, renamed Cephas, who denies Jesus; the same individual across all four Gospels and Acts.

clusters.name: Simon the Pharisee
clusters.note: Pharisee host who rebukes the sinful woman at dinner; not the fisherman.

clusters.name: Simon Magus
clusters.note: Samaritan sorcerer who offers money for the Spirit; not Peter.

clusters.name: Simon the tanner
clusters.note: Tanner in Joppa whose house Peter lodges in; distinct from Peter and Simon Magus.

clusters.name: Andrew
clusters.note: Fisherman from Bethsaida, brother of Simon Peter, one of the first disciples and the twelve; the same individual in the Gospels, and a name-only apostle in Acts.

clusters.name: James son of Zebedee
clusters.note: Fisherman apostle, brother of John, present at the transfiguration and Gethsemane; the same individual in the Gospels and in Acts 12.

clusters.name: James the brother of Jesus
clusters.note: Leader of the Jerusalem assembly in Acts 15 and 21; distinct from James son of Zebedee.

clusters.name: Judas Iscariot
clusters.note: The apostle who keeps the money box and betrays Jesus; the same individual across the Gospels and Acts 1.

clusters.name: Judas (not Iscariot)
clusters.note: Disciple who asks at the supper why Jesus will reveal himself only to the disciples; distinct from the betrayer.

clusters.name: Philip the apostle
clusters.note: One of the twelve from Bethsaida who brings Nathanael and the Greeks to Jesus; the same apostle in Matthew, Luke, John and the Acts upper room list.

clusters.name: Philip the evangelist
clusters.note: One of the seven who preaches in Samaria and baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch; distinct from the apostle.

clusters.name: Thomas
clusters.note: Apostle called Didymus who doubts the resurrection until he sees Jesus; the fourth disciple named in John 21:2 is the same person.

clusters.name: Bartholomew
clusters.note: Apostle named only in the twelve-apostle lists; the same individual in each list.

clusters.name: James son of Alphaeus
clusters.note: Apostle named only in the twelve-apostle lists; distinct from James son of Zebedee.

clusters.name: Simon the Zealot
clusters.note: Apostle named only in the twelve-apostle lists; distinct from Simon Peter.

clusters.name: Caiaphas
clusters.note: High priest who plots Jesus' death and presides at his trial; the same individual in Matthew, John and Acts 4.

clusters.name: Pontius Pilate
clusters.note: Roman governor of Judea who tries Jesus and orders his crucifixion; the same individual across the Gospels and Acts.

clusters.name: Barabbas
clusters.note: Prisoner or robber released in place of Jesus; the same individual in all three Gospels.

clusters.name: Roman soldiers
clusters.note: Roman soldiers who mock, flog and crucify Jesus and guard the tomb, in the Gospels; the guards at the tomb are the same soldiers.

clusters.name: Herod's soldiers
clusters.note: Soldiers guarding Peter in prison in Acts 12; a separate body from the Gospel soldiers.

clusters.name: Centurion of Capernaum
clusters.note: Roman officer whose servant Jesus heals at a distance; in Matthew 8 and Luke 7 this is one individual.

clusters.name: Centurion at the cross
clusters.note: Officer who watches the crucifixion and declares Jesus the Son of God; a separate officer in each Gospel, identified as the same as the Capernaum centurion only by Matthew's link.

clusters.name: Joseph of Arimathea
clusters.note: Rich or secret disciple who buries Jesus in his new tomb; the same individual in Matthew and John.

clusters.name: Simon of Cyrene
clusters.note: Man compelled to carry Jesus' cross; distinct from Simon Peter.

clusters.name: The leper
clusters.note: Man healed of leprosy by Jesus; the same healing story in Matthew 8 and Luke 5.

clusters.name: The paralytic
clusters.note: Paralyzed man carried to Jesus, forgiven and healed; the same healing story in Matthew 9 and Luke 5.

clusters.name: The disciples
clusters.note: Jesus' followers as a body in Matthew and John.

clusters.name: Caesar Augustus
clusters.note: Roman emperor whose census decree opens Luke's birth narrative; a different Caesar appears in Acts.

clusters.name: Caesar (emperor in Acts)
clusters.note: Unnamed Roman emperor to whom Paul appeals in Acts 25; not Augustus of Luke 2.

clusters.name: Judas son of James
clusters.note: Apostle named in the twelve lists and Acts 1; the same individual in both.

clusters.name: Martha
clusters.note: Sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany who serves Jesus; the same woman in Luke 10 and John.

clusters.name: Lazarus the beggar
clusters.note: Poor beggar in Jesus' parable of the rich man, carried to Abraham's bosom; a parable figure, not the man raised from the dead.

clusters.name: Lazarus of Bethany
clusters.note: Brother of Martha and Mary, raised from the tomb after four days; appears only in John.

clusters.name: The nobleman in the parable of the minas
clusters.note: Nobleman in Luke's parable who goes to receive a kingdom; a parable figure.

clusters.name: The nobleman at Capernaum
clusters.note: Royal official whose son Jesus heals from a distance in John 4.

clusters.name: Joseph called Barsabbas
clusters.note: Candidate put forward with Matthias to replace Judas in Acts 1; not chosen. Distinct from Justus of Corinth.

clusters.name: Justus of Corinth
clusters.note: Corinthian host next door to the synagogue in Acts 18; not the same as Joseph called Barsabbas.

clusters.name: Annas the high priest
clusters.note: Elder high priest at the trial of Peter and John in Acts 4; the one name given in these passages.

clusters.name: Judas of Galilee
clusters.note: Rebel leader of the census days, named in Gamaliel's speech; never on stage.

clusters.name: Cornelius the centurion
clusters.note: Roman centurion of the Italian cohort at Caesarea whose vision brings Peter to his house in Acts 10.

clusters.name: Prophets and teachers of Antioch
clusters.note: The collective group of Antioch leaders who set apart Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13:1-3.

clusters.name: Simeon called Niger
clusters.note: Antioch prophet named in Acts 13:1, called Niger.

clusters.name: Lucius of Cyrene
clusters.note: Antioch prophet named in Acts 13:1, from Cyrene.

clusters.name: Manaen
clusters.note: Antioch prophet named in Acts 13:1, foster brother of Herod the tetrarch.

clusters.name: Gaius of Macedonia
clusters.note: Macedonian companion of Paul seized in the Ephesian theater riot, Acts 19:29; not Gaius of Derbe.

clusters.name: Gaius of Derbe
clusters.note: Companion of Paul from Derbe listed in Acts 20:4; not Gaius of Macedonia.

clusters.name: Ephesian Jews at the synagogue
clusters.note: Synagogue audience in Ephesus who ask Paul to stay (Acts 18-19), including the hardened listeners who speak evil of the Way.

clusters.name: Babel
clusters.note: Site of the tower on the plain of Shinar in Genesis 11, also an early city of Nimrod's kingdom; Babylon is the same region in Acts.

clusters.name: Haran
clusters.note: City in northern Mesopotamia where Terah dies and Abram stays for a time; distinct from the wider Mesopotamia region.

clusters.name: Paddan Aram
clusters.note: Region of Haran where Laban lives and Jacob marries and has children; the Mesopotamia of Genesis.

clusters.name: Mesopotamia and Haran (Acts)
clusters.note: Places where God calls Abraham in Stephen's speech, Acts 7:2-4.

clusters.name: Egypt (Genesis, Joseph and Abram)
clusters.note: The land of Abram's famine visit and of Joseph's rule and the family's settlement, Genesis 12 and 37-50.

clusters.name: Egypt (Exodus, bondage and plagues)
clusters.note: The land of Israel's enslavement and the plagues, Exodus.

clusters.name: Egypt (Matthew, refuge)
clusters.note: Place of refuge for the holy family in Matthew 2.

clusters.name: Egypt (Acts, Stephen and Paul)
clusters.note: Land of Joseph and Moses recounted in Acts 7 and 13.

clusters.name: Shechem
clusters.note: City in Canaan where Jacob buys land and Dinah is defiled, Genesis 33-37.

clusters.name: Shechem tomb (Acts)
clusters.note: Burial place of Jacob and the fathers, Acts 7:16.

clusters.name: Goshen (Genesis)
clusters.note: Region of Egypt where Jacob's family settles, Genesis 45-50.

clusters.name: Goshen (Exodus)
clusters.note: Region of Egypt where Israel dwells apart during the plagues of flies, hail and darkness.

clusters.name: Mount Sinai
clusters.note: Mountain where Yahweh gives the law in Exodus, also called Horeb.

clusters.name: Mount Sinai (Acts)
clusters.note: Mountain where the angel speaks to Moses, Acts 7:30-38.

clusters.name: The wilderness (Exodus)
clusters.note: Desert between Egypt and the mountain where Israel wanders, fed with manna.

clusters.name: The wilderness (Luke)
clusters.note: Desert where John preaches and Jesus is tempted.

clusters.name: The wilderness forty years (Acts)
clusters.note: Desert of Israel's forty years in Stephen's and Paul's speeches.

clusters.name: Ashdod
clusters.note: Philistine city where the ark is placed in Dagon's temple, 1 Samuel 5.

clusters.name: Azotus
clusters.note: Town where Philip reappears in Acts 8:40; the same town as Ashdod.

clusters.name: Bethlehem (Samuel)
clusters.note: Home of Jesse and David where Samuel anoints David.

clusters.name: Bethlehem (Matthew and Luke)
clusters.note: Town where Jesus is born, in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke.

clusters.name: Jerusalem
clusters.note: The holy city with the temple, the main city of action across the Gospels and Acts.

clusters.name: Nazareth
clusters.note: Galilean town where Joseph and Mary settle and Jesus is raised.

clusters.name: The Jordan
clusters.note: River where John baptizes and Jesus is baptized.

clusters.name: Capernaum
clusters.note: Galilean town on the sea where Jesus lives and teaches and heals.

clusters.name: The mountain of the sermon (Matthew)
clusters.note: Hillside where the sermon on the mount is preached, Matthew 5-7.

clusters.name: The mountain of transfiguration (Luke)
clusters.note: Mountain where Jesus is transfigured with Moses and Elijah, Luke 9.

clusters.name: The temple in Jerusalem
clusters.note: The temple in Jerusalem where Jesus teaches, cleanses, and is presented; the Acts temple courts are the same building.

clusters.name: Solomon's porch
clusters.note: Colonnade of the temple where the crowd gathers around Peter, Acts 3 and 5.

clusters.name: The Mount of Olives
clusters.note: Hill east of Jerusalem where Jesus teaches and prays, and from which he ascends in Acts 1.

clusters.name: The Praetorium
clusters.note: Roman governor's headquarters where Pilate tries and mocks Jesus.

clusters.name: Golgotha
clusters.note: Hill outside Jerusalem where Jesus is crucified.

clusters.name: Joseph's tomb
clusters.note: Rock-cut tomb of Joseph of Arimathaea where Jesus is laid and later found empty; the same tomb in both Matthew and Luke.

clusters.name: Bethany (near Jerusalem)
clusters.note: Village near Jerusalem home of Lazarus, Mary and Martha, where Jesus is anointed and ascends; one village across all three Gospels.

clusters.name: Jericho
clusters.note: City on the road from Jerusalem where blind men are healed and Zacchaeus lives; a single city across the Gospels.

clusters.name: Galilee (northern region and sea)
clusters.note: Northern region where Jesus grows up and ministers; in John it includes the Sea of Galilee, the same region as in the other Gospels and Acts.

clusters.name: Judea (southern region)
clusters.note: Southern region including Jerusalem; the same region in Luke and Acts.

clusters.name: Samaria (region)
clusters.note: Region of the Samaritans, where Jesus meets a villager and lepers and where Philip preaches in Acts; the same region across Luke and Acts.

clusters.name: Sychar in Samaria
clusters.note: Samaritan town by Jacob's well where Jesus meets the woman at the well; a specific town in John, distinct from the region of Samaria.

brief.tone: Reverent and varied: the mood shifts across the work from primordial solemnity and sacred dread through intimate family drama, prophetic tension, luminous grace in the Gospels, and hopeful urgency in the spread of the early church.
depiction_rules: God the Father is never given a human face or body; show divine presence through light, voice, cloud, fire, or a hand where tradition permits.
Angels appear as luminous human-like messengers, not winged figures unless the scene calls for it.
Violence, including crucifixion, stoning and beheading, is shown with weight and dignity, without gratuitous gore.
Nudity and sexual shame (Noah, Lot, Saul prophesying naked) are covered, turned away, or handled with restraint.
Idols such as the golden calf, Dagon and teraphim are shown as objects, never as divine presence.
The Holy Spirit appears only as a dove, wind, or tongues of fire, where the text names it.
Jesus is always identifiable as a 1st-century Jewish man, avoiding later halo-and-robe stereotypes unless the scene demands it.
Religious opponents, crowds and Judas are drawn with individual dignity and varied expressions, never as caricatures.

eras.name: Ancient Near East: primeval, patriarchal and Egyptian bronze-age world
eras.people: Semitic herders, farmers and city dwellers; Egyptians, Canaanites, Philistines and Hittites; dark-haired, bearded men and veiled women.
eras.dress: Simple linen and wool tunics, robes, cloaks and sandals; Egyptian officials in fine linen with gold chains.
eras.buildings_and_objects: Mud-brick cities such as Ur, goat-hair tents, stone altars, wells, flocks, camels, donkeys and Egyptian chariots.
eras.technology: Bronze and early iron tools, pottery, weaving; no firearms or metal coins; silver weighed by the shekel.

eras.name: Exodus, wilderness and early Israel
eras.people: Egyptians with shaven heads, wigs and linen kilts; Hebrew clans in plain desert clothing; Midianite shepherds; Israelite tribes as farmers and herders in hill country.
eras.dress: Linen kilts for Egyptians; woven wool for Israelites; priestly blue, purple and scarlet linen with ephod and breastplate; bronze helmets and mail for warriors.
eras.buildings_and_objects: Brick storage cities, portable tabernacle, stone altars, Shiloh's gates, wooden ark overlaid with gold, threshing floors, strongholds, papyrus baskets and staves.
eras.technology: Brickmaking with straw, bronze and gold metalwork, chariots and horses, emerging iron weapons; stone-tablet writing; weights instead of coins.

eras.name: First-century Roman Judea, Galilee and the wider empire
eras.people: Jewish villagers, fishermen, shepherds, priests, Pharisees, tax collectors, Samaritans, Gentiles, Greeks and Roman soldiers and officials; olive to dark-haired, tanned Mediterranean people.
eras.dress: Linen and wool tunics, fringed cloaks and mantles, head coverings and veils, sandals; priests in white linen; Roman soldiers in armor; wealthy in purple and fine linen; sailors in short tunics.
eras.buildings_and_objects: Flat-roofed stone and mud-brick houses, village synagogues, the Jerusalem temple, rock-cut tombs with rolled stones, Roman barracks and governors' palaces, Greek theaters, oil lamps, clay jars, boats, nets, vineyards, scrolls and letters.
eras.technology: Oil lamps and torches, sailing and oared ships, ox carts and chariots, hand mills, denarii and shekels, Roman roads; scrolls and parchment writing; no printing, clocks or firearms.
